title: Child asks 'why remember?': forget-by memory leases with recompute recipes
idea: A child asks why you'd keep every toy out forever. So each allocation carries a forget-by lease and a lineage recipe: the function and input handles that produced it. On expiry or memory pressure the OS drops the page and keeps only the recipe, and a later touch faults and recomputes it. This is Spark-RDD lineage moved down into virtual memory, aimed at caches, memo tables, decoded assets and derived indexes.
why: Derived data is often 30-50% of resident memory. Making it recompute-on-demand cuts resident DRAM 20-40% for cache-heavy services, paid for with spare CPU cycles.

title: Alien who sees only entropy: entropy-sized frames in CXL expander
idea: An alien observer sees information content, not 4 KB pages. A CXL Type-3 controller measures each incoming page's compressibility inline and stores it in a 512 B, 1 KB, 2 KB or 4 KB slot. A sub-page indirection table and per-class free lists track the slots, so the host sees full nominal capacity while the media holds only the entropy.
why: Server memory typically compresses 2-3x. Transparent entropy-sized storage gives 1.8-2.5x effective capacity per DRAM chip with zero OS changes, attacking cost per bit.

title: 2050 engineer: KV cache stored as per-sequence implicit neural field
idea: A 2050 engineer stores functions, not tables. For each long sequence, a tiny sinusoidal MLP per layer is fitted online to map (position, head) to the K/V vector and refitted incrementally every few hundred tokens, and attention queries this field instead of a table. Exact KV is kept only for the recent window and for outlier tokens the field reconstructs poorly.
why: KV cache dominates long-context inference memory. A 20-50x fit on older tokens would turn 1M-token contexts from hundreds of GB into a few GB. The accuracy risk is high.

title: Biologist's genome thinking: grow embeddings from hashed IDs, not tables
idea: A genome stores the recipe, not the organism. Recommendation and retrieval embedding tables, often terabytes, are replaced by a generator: several universal hashes of an ID feed a small dense MLP that expresses the embedding on demand. An exact side table remains only for the hottest ~0.1% of IDs.
why: Embedding tables are the largest DRAM consumers in ad and recsys fleets. Generator embeddings shrink them 100-1000x for ~1-3% extra FLOPs, moving cost from scarce DRAM to cheap compute.

title: Apollo core-rope weaver: frozen weights in via-programmed ROM chiplets
idea: Apollo's flight software was literally woven into core-rope ROM. Production model weights that won't change for a year are mask-programmed into dense, multi-bit, stackable via-ROM chiplets on a mature node and co-packaged beside the accelerator. HBM then holds only KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are 50-80% of inference HBM. ROM needs no capacitor, no refresh and no EUV, and it can be made in 28-40 nm US fabs. That frees most HBM for KV cache and attacks capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Mapmaker's zoom levels: bit-plane tiering of tensors across memory tiers
idea: A mapmaker never prints every street at world scale. Weights and KV are stored transposed into bit-planes: the top 3-4 planes live in HBM and the low-order planes in CXL DRAM or flash. Matmuls run on the coarse planes first and fetch fine planes only for rows whose partial results sit near a decision boundary, such as attention top-k or softmax peaks.
why: Most scores are decided by the MSBs, so HBM capacity per model drops 2-4x and HBM traffic drops roughly in proportion.

title: Game texture artist: store tensors in GPU texture compression formats
idea: Game artists have shipped fixed-rate block-compressed textures (BC/ASTC) for decades, and GPU texture units decode them for free. Weights and cached activations are packed as 4x4 blocks in an ASTC-like fixed-rate tensor format and read through the otherwise idle texture-sampling path, which decompresses at line rate with random access and no indirection tables.
why: This gives a fixed 3-6x compression with random access and no ALU cost, using silicon already on every GPU. HBM capacity and bandwidth per model shrink by the same factor.

title: Octopus arms think locally: filtering engines inside CXL memory modules
idea: Two-thirds of an octopus's neurons sit in its arms. Each CXL memory module gets a small engine for scan, filter, hash-probe and gather, so analytics and database operators run where the data sits and return only results. That eliminates the host-side staging buffers, decoded copies and hash tables that currently mirror the data in local DRAM.
why: Analytics nodes often hold 2-3 copies of hot data (raw, decoded and intermediate). Near-data operators cut host DRAM 30-60% and also cut data-movement energy.

title: Neuroscientist's predictive brain: store only prediction residuals in memory controller
idea: The cortex mostly transmits prediction errors. The memory controller runs cheap per-line predictors (stride, delta from the neighboring line, or the previous version of the line) and stores just the residual plus a 2-bit predictor tag. This is video motion compensation applied to arrays, page tables, counters and timestamps.
why: Numeric arrays and pointers are highly predictable. Residual coding gets 2-4x on exactly the data where dictionary and LZ methods fail, raising effective capacity per bit.

title: Homeric bard's formulas: fleet-trained compression dictionaries in memory controllers
idea: Oral poets held whole epics in memory as reusable formulas ('rosy-fingered dawn'). A hyperscaler mines fleet memory for recurring 16-64 B fragments (object headers, vtable pointers, UTF-8 strings, protobuf tags) and trains a shared dictionary per workload class. Memory-controller compressors load it and replace the fragments with short codes.
why: On small 64 B lines, shared dictionaries beat per-line compressors by about 1.5-2x. That is +30-60% effective DRAM capacity fleet-wide.

title: Artist's negative space: VM pages stored as diffs against rack-golden images
idea: Painters define a shape by what is missing. One golden copy of each common OS and runtime image lives in rack-shared CXL memory. Each VM page is stored as a sparse XOR or byte-diff delta against its matching golden page, found by content hash at boot and by background scanning.
why: VMs share 70-90% near-identical pages that differ by a few bytes, which exact dedup misses. Delta storage reclaims 15-30% of host DRAM in VM-dense racks.

title: Linguist's Zipf law: precision proportional to word frequency
idea: Linguists know a few words carry most usage. Embedding and output-projection rows are sorted by token or ID frequency and quantized on a log-frequency schedule: 8-bit for the top 1%, 4-bit for the next 10%, and 2-bit codebooks for the long tail, with a learned scale per tier.
why: Rare rows contribute little loss, so vocabulary and embedding tables shrink 3-5x with negligible quality impact. This matters for 256k-vocabulary LLMs and recsys.

title: Developmental biologist: thousands of fine-tunes as epigenetic bit-masks
idea: Every cell shares one genome and differs only in which genes are switched on. Thousands of fine-tuned variants are served from one base copy in HBM. Each variant is stored as a run-length-coded sparse sign-flip/zero mask of about 0.1 bit per parameter or less, applied on the fly inside the matmul kernel.
why: This replaces per-tenant full copies or large adapters. 1,000 variants of a 70B model fit in roughly the memory of 1.1 copies, a 100x+ saving for multi-tenant serving.

title: ER triage nurse: three-tier KV precision with a sink summary token
idea: Triage sorts patients by urgency. Every 256 tokens, accumulated attention mass ranks the cached tokens. Critical tokens stay FP8, stable ones are requantized to 2-bit, and the rest are evicted after their values are folded into a running weighted 'sink' token per head, so their aggregate influence survives.
why: KV memory drops 4-8x at long context with less quality loss than pure eviction, which means more concurrent users per GPU.

title: Navigator's dead reckoning: cross-layer KV stored as deltas from fixes
idea: A navigator takes a full position fix occasionally and dead-reckons between fixes. Full KV is stored only for every 4th layer (the fix). The intermediate layers' KV is stored as low-rank deltas against the nearest fix and reconstructed inside the attention kernel.
why: In deep models, adjacent-layer KV differences are low-rank, giving 2.5-3.5x KV memory savings in long-context decode.

title: Holographer's superposition: bind thousands of key-value pairs into shared vectors
idea: A hologram spreads the whole scene across every fragment. Distant-past key-value pairs are bound by circular convolution (holographic reduced representations) and summed into a fixed bank of 64 superposition vectors per head. A query unbinds them by correlation to retrieve an approximate value, while recent tokens stay exact.
why: Memory for the distant past becomes O(1) per head instead of O(n), aimed at 10M-token agent memories. Retrieval noise grows with load.

title: Mycologist's spores: hibernate idle AI agents as compressed snapshots
idea: Fungi survive lean times as tiny spores. Agent sessions spend most of their wall-clock time waiting on users or tools. After ~2 s idle, the session's KV cache, runtime heap and sandbox are snapshotted into a compressed, deduplicated spore on NVMe and rehydrated in tens of ms by lazily paging in only the pages touched first.
why: Agent fleets keep thousands of mostly idle sessions resident. Spores cut resident DRAM/HBM per concurrent agent 10-20x.

title: Embargoed Soviet engineer: 32-bit compressed pointers everywhere via cage allocator
idea: Under embargo you rewrite the software to fit the machine you have. Compilers and allocators place each heap in a 4-32 GB 'cage' and store all heap pointers as shifted 32-bit offsets. The JVM and V8 already do this; a compiler flag plus ABI shim extends it to C++, Rust and Go.
why: Pointers are 20-40% of the heap in pointer-heavy services (graphs, trees, ORMs). Halving them cuts DRAM 10-25% fleet-wide with no new hardware.

title: Cartoon animator's keyframes: video-model activations as keyframes plus sparse deltas
idea: Animators draw keyframes and let assistants fill the in-betweens. In video-generation and world-model serving, full per-frame KV and activations are kept only for keyframes every 8 frames. Other frames store sparse top-k token deltas against the nearest keyframe, since consecutive latents differ in only a few percent of tokens.
why: Video-model memory scales with frames x tokens. A 4-8x reduction makes minute-long generation fit on a single node.

title: Desert camel's stored fat: lossless entropy-coded weights decoded in shared memory
idea: A camel carries dense fat and converts it to water only when needed. BF16 weights live in HBM with the low-entropy exponent field Huffman-coded and the mantissa left raw. Each kernel decodes its tile into SM shared memory just before the matmul, so expanded weights never exist in DRAM.
why: The exponent carries about 2-3 bits of entropy out of 8, giving ~30% bit-exact compression with zero accuracy risk. Memory-bound decode also speeds up.

title: Migratory birds follow the sun: shift memory-heavy services across time zones
idea: Birds don't winter where food is scarce. A global scheduler moves memory-hungry, latency-tolerant work (batch inference, embedding refreshes, index builds, prefix-KV warmups) each day to the regions at their nightly trough. Each region's DRAM is then sized for its own interactive peak rather than the sum of all peaks.
why: Diurnal swings of 30-50% mean pooling in time cuts total provisioned DRAM 15-25% with no new hardware.

title: Alien with no CPU/memory split: attention computed in HBM logic die
idea: An alien that never separated thinking from remembering would score attention and accumulate values in the HBM base die. KV is stored in a 2-bit grouped format that only the in-stack PIM reads: dequantization and softmax happen beside the banks, and only the attended output vector leaves the stack.
why: KV capacity per stack rises 4-8x and KV traffic leaves the interposer, attacking both data-movement energy (3-4 pJ/bit) and capacity.

title: Mole lives underground: vector search fully inside SSD controllers
idea: A mole never needs the surface. Billion-scale vector indexes (a graph ANN plus PQ codes, normally hundreds of GB of DRAM) live entirely on SSDs whose controllers walk the graph and compute PQ distances internally. The host keeps only a tiny entry-point table and receives top-k IDs.
why: This removes 90%+ of the DRAM in RAG and vector-database servers, where DRAM now costs ~20-40x flash per byte, at retrieval-acceptable millisecond latency.

title: Embargoed Soviet tinkerer: CXL tier built from scrapped DDR4 DIMMs
idea: With no new chips available, the tinkerer reuses old ones. Off-the-shelf FPGA CXL boards (~$5-10k each) each host 8-16 decommissioned DDR4 RDIMMs, burned in and binned by error rate, and expose them as a CXL Type-3 warm tier; firmware adds patrol scrubbing and thermal throttling. Budget: ~$400k for boards and lab, ~$600k for two FPGA/firmware engineers over 24 months.
why: Hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 DIMMs. Reclaimed bits cost ~5-10% of new DDR5 at shortage prices and add 1.5-2x capacity per server for warm data.

title: Child says share your toys: one host copy of weights
idea: A child asks why ten pods load the same model ten times. An open-source daemon pins each model file once per host in hugepage-backed shared memory, and patched vLLM, TGI and PyTorch loaders mmap it read-only instead of keeping private host-RAM copies for staging, CPU offload and fast restart. Two engineers, ~9 months, ~$400k.
why: Inference hosts hold 4-8 duplicate host-RAM copies of the same weights. Dedup frees hundreds of GB per node, so cheaper host SKUs can be bought.

title: Farmer's almanac: seasonal working-set forecasts drive safe memory overcommit
idea: Farmers plant by the almanac. A controller learns each VM or pod's daily and weekly working-set seasonality from sampled PTE access bits and overcommits hosts to the forecast plus a margin. A zswap/CXL compressed tier acts as the 'frost guard' that absorbs mispredictions. It ships as open-source KVM and Kubernetes plugins with a 3-person team within $1M.
why: Allocated memory averages 40-60% utilization. Forecast-based overcommit reaches 1.3-1.6x effective capacity per DIMM.

title: Accountant's shadow price: bill every team DRAM at 2026 spot
idea: An accountant makes hidden costs visible. A chargeback tool reads each service's resident GB-hours from cgroup stats and bills them at the current 4x contract price in dashboards, PR comments and quarterly budgets, with a savings leaderboard. The tool costs under $300k; the rest of the budget funds pilots at three companies.
why: Once memory is a visible line item, teams typically cut 15-30% within a year through heap caps, cache sizing and replica trimming. It is a policy lever with near-zero capital.

title: Seed-bank keeper: pages stored as generator plus seed
idea: A seed bank stores seeds, not forests. A userfaultfd library lets programs register regions produced by deterministic generators (PRNG noise, dropout masks, random projections, synthetic test data, procedurally initialized tensors) as (generator ID, seed, offset). Under pressure the pages are dropped, and on a fault they are regenerated bit-exactly with vectorized Philox at >10 GB/s.
why: Random data defeats every compressor yet has near-zero Kolmogorov size. This frees tens of GB per training or simulation node for about $300k of engineering.

title: Tailor's made-to-measure: compiler narrows struct fields to observed ranges
idea: A tailor cuts cloth to the body, not a standard size. An LLVM plugin profiles field value ranges in production and rewrites hot structs with bit-packed narrow fields (int64 to int20, enums to 3 bits, pointers to 32-bit indices). A cheap overflow check migrates an object to a wide spill layout if a value ever exceeds its range. Three compiler engineers can do it in 24 months.
why: Typical C++/Rust structs are 30-50% padding and over-wide fields, so this cuts the heap 20-35% on data-structure-heavy services.

title: Monk with one bowl: eBPF census finds duplicate buffer copies
idea: A monk owns one bowl, not five. An eBPF plus page-hash census tool samples contents across the page cache, socket buffers, user heaps and GPU staging buffers and flags identical data held in two or more places (the NIC-kernel-user-serialize-GPU chain). The team then ships upstream zero-copy patches (io_uring registered buffers, splice, mmap'd page cache) for the top offenders.
why: Data-path services hold 2-5 copies of in-flight data. A small team can free 10-25% of DRAM on storage, proxy and ingest nodes.

title: Tetris player clears lines: mesh fragmented pages without moving objects
idea: A Tetris player clears half-empty rows. A meshing allocator finds two virtual pages whose live objects don't overlap in offset, copies one into the other, and remaps both virtual pages to the same physical frame, freeing a frame without changing any pointer. A fleet fragmentation profiler proves the payoff, and the work fits well under $1M.
why: Long-running C/C++ servers lose 15-30% of RSS to fragmentation. Meshing recovers 10-20% with no application code changes.

title: Grandmother's leftovers: reuse cached document KV across different prompts
idea: Grandma turns yesterday's roast into today's soup. RAG documents are pre-encoded once into KV chunks stored on NVMe by content hash. At request time the retrieved chunks are spliced into the prompt's KV in any order, and only the ~10-15% of tokens at chunk boundaries or with high deviation are recomputed to repair cross-chunk attention. Software only, two engineers.
why: This removes duplicate KV for the same documents across thousands of requests and cuts prefill. RAG fleets see 3-5x less KV memory churn.

title: Librarian's closed stacks: garbage collector exiles cold objects to NVMe
idea: Libraries keep rarely requested books in closed stacks. A modified generational GC (OpenJDK or Go) samples object reads with 1% read barriers. Objects untouched for N collections are compacted into closed-stack regions and madvised out to NVMe, with forwarding pointers so a touch faults back the whole batch. Fundable as a 24-month, 3-person project.
why: Managed heaps are sized 2-3x their live data and hold large cold populations. Object-granular exile cuts heap DRAM 25-50% and beats page-level swap on mixed hot/cold pages.

title: Ant colony's pheromone trails: route requests to replicas holding their prefix
idea: Ants follow pheromone to where the food already is. An inference router keeps a decaying radix-tree sketch (the 'pheromone') of which prompt prefixes each replica holds and sends each request to the longest match, balanced against load. Each shared prefix is then cached once per fleet instead of once per replica. A few engineer-months.
why: Fleets with long shared system prompts duplicate prefix KV on every replica. Affinity routing cuts aggregate KV memory 2-5x.

title: Air traffic controller assigns landing slots by predicted output length
idea: Controllers schedule landings so the runway is never overbooked. A small classifier predicts each request's output length from the prompt. The scheduler reserves KV pages for the predicted trajectory and packs requests to ~95% peak occupancy instead of sizing for the worst case, preempting by swap only on mispredictions. Software only.
why: Conservative KV reservation wastes 30-60% of HBM. Predicted landing slots raise concurrency per GB 1.5-2x.

title: Kintsugi potter repairs cracks: reuse DIMMs with known-bad rows
idea: Kintsugi makes cracked pottery whole and valuable. A ~$50k automated tester maps the failing rows of scrapped or factory-reject DIMMs and writes the bad-row map into a small SPD/EEPROM sidecar. A Linux boot-time driver reads the map and permanently retires those pages, so each DIMM serves ~99.9% of its capacity.
why: Many field returns and test rejects fail in only a handful of rows. Reclaiming them adds usable supply at ~zero silicon cost and also cuts e-waste.

title: Soviet-style socialist competition: bounties for memory-footprint patches
idea: Like a five-year-plan competition, but paid. A $600k bounty pool pays per verified GB saved on standard benchmarks of the 50 most-deployed open-source infrastructure packages (Postgres, Redis, Kafka, Elasticsearch, PyTorch DataLoader, Chromium). A $400k CI harness measures peak and steady RSS before and after each merged patch.
why: Code that runs on millions of servers multiplies every saving: a 10% footprint cut in these packages frees millions of GB globally, which may be the highest-leverage use of $1M.

title: Parent reading food labels: memory-footprint labels in software procurement
idea: Parents compare nutrition labels. An open 'Memory Facts' label (peak RSS, steady-state RSS per 1k users, bytes per stored record) is measured by a reference harness, and the campaign gets federal and large-enterprise procurement (GSA, state CIOs) to require it, as Energy Star did for power. Costs: standards work, the harness and outreach.
why: Buyer pressure pushes memory efficiency across the software supply chain, and 5-10% footprint cuts per procurement cycle compound.

title: Genome Project biologist: open atlas of real memory contents
idea: Biology took off once the genome was sequenced. An opt-in agent samples hashed, entropy-profiled page snapshots (never raw data) from volunteer fleets and publishes a 'memory atlas': the share of zero pages, duplicates, near-duplicates, compressible types, pointer density and cold data by workload. About $800k.
why: Outside three hyperscalers, nobody knows where the reclaimable bytes are. The atlas aims every compression, dedup and tiering effort at the biggest wins, priming 20-40% savings.

title: 2050 engineer laughing at boxed integers: unboxed CPython containers
idea: A 2050 engineer finds 28-byte Python ints absurd. A CPython extension, later an upstream PEP, gives lists and dicts lazily specialized storage: a container holding only ints, floats or short ASCII strings switches to a packed unboxed array or arena and boxes values only on access, invisibly to user code. Two core developers, 24 months.
why: Python data-processing heaps are 4-10x the raw data size. Specialized containers cut DRAM 2-5x in ETL jobs, ML data loaders and web caches.

title: Teen texter's abbreviations: superword tokenizer adapter shrinks KV per document
idea: Teens write 'brb' for 'be right back'. An open model's tokenizer gains ~50k frequent multi-word tokens, and only the new embedding rows plus a light LoRA are trained (~$200k of compute). The same text then needs 25-35% fewer tokens, so it needs 25-35% fewer KV entries.
why: KV memory and prefill scale linearly with token count, so a 30% token cut is 30% less KV at any context length, and it stacks with quantization.

title: Haiku poet's compression: distill long system prompts into gist tokens
idea: A haiku holds a scene in 17 syllables. A deployment's fixed 2-10k-token system prompt or tool manifest is distilled into 16-64 learned soft 'gist' tokens. Only those embeddings are trained, to match the model's outputs under the full prompt. The GPU cost is hundreds of dollars per deployment.
why: Agentic apps carry huge fixed prompts on every request. Gisting cuts per-request prefix KV and prefill by ~100x.

title: Demoscene 64k coder: neural texture compression plugin for game engines
idea: Demosceners fit whole worlds in 64 KB. An Unreal/Godot plugin encodes each material's texture stack (albedo, normal, roughness and more) into a small latent grid plus a tiny MLP decoded in the shader at sample time, replacing block-compressed mip chains. A 4-person team can build it in 24 months.
why: Textures are 50-70% of game and VR memory. Neural textures give 4-8x over BCn, letting consoles, PCs and headsets ship with less DRAM.

title: Construction foreman's just-in-time delivery: router-lookahead MoE expert paging
idea: Foremen have steel delivered the day it is bolted up. A small predictor reads layer L's hidden state and forecasts which experts layers L+1 to L+3 will route to. Those experts are DMA'd from host RAM or NVMe via GPUDirect Storage just in time, and HBM keeps only a hot-expert cache. Software-only, open-source.
why: MoE models keep every expert resident while each token uses ~5% of them. Lookahead paging cuts weight HBM 3-6x for open MoE models on commodity GPUs.

title: Insurance actuary prices risk: discounted VMs with memory-pressure insurance
idea: Actuaries price rare events. A cloud or colo sells VMs 25% cheaper whose guests agree that during rare host pressure events up to 30% of their pages may be served from a compressed tier. Credits ('claims') are paid automatically per minute of measured degradation. Billing and telemetry software fits in the budget.
why: Pricing overcommit turns a hidden risk into a product, so providers can safely run 1.3-1.5x memory overcommit.

title: Scrap-metal dealer: memory-recovery contractor paid in reclaimed gigabytes
idea: Scrap dealers profit from what others throw away. A 6-person firm audits client fleets (heap dumps, page census, configs), applies the fixes, and keeps 30% of the first year's avoided DRAM purchases, verified by telemetry. The $1M covers runway until the first two contracts pay.
why: Most enterprises have 20-40% reclaimable memory but no team to get it. At 4x prices, gain-sharing makes adoption risk-free and unlocks supply without fabs.
